reasoning.Student A:
I will report my true preferences because, under the standard student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism used in many school-choice settings, it is a dominant strategy for students to rank schools truthfully. Misrepresenting preferences cannot yield a strictly better outcome and can only risk a worse one.

Concretely for my situation:
- My sincere ranking is x > y > w > z.
- I have high priority (rank 1) at w and y and lower priority (rank 2) at x and z.
- Many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y will be competitive. However, since I prefer x to y I should still list x first; if I am displaced at x I have good fallback at y because I have top priority there.
- Listing a less-preferred school ahead of a more-preferred one (to try to “game” priorities) is unnecessary and risky because DA is strategy-proof for students.

Therefore I will submit the complete ranking in my sincere order.
reasoning.Student B:
I should submit preferences that maximize my chance of getting the best feasible school. Under the usual student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism, truthful reporting is a dominant strategy, so I should list my true ranking. Even without that guarantee, given the information about others' rankings (most favor y first) and my priorities, it is strategic to put x first:

- My true top choice is x and I have priority 1 at x, so I am well-positioned to get x if I rank it first.
- I also have priority 1 at z and prefer z to y, while most other applicants rank z last, so z is relatively safe as my second choice.
- Many others favor y first and I have lower priority (2) at y, so ranking y ahead of x or z risks losing those higher-priority applicants for a crowded y; better to place y after x and z.
- w is my least preferred and I have lower priority there, so it belongs last.

Therefore I will submit my true ranking: x > z > y > w.
reasoning.Student C: I rank truthfully but with strategic reasoning: my true preference is x > w > z > y. Most applicants favor y first, and my priority at y is low (4), so I'm unlikely to get y if many higher-priority applicants apply there. I have better priority (3) at both x and w, so listing x first maximizes my chance at my top choice; listing w second keeps a strong backup where I also have decent priority. Between z and y I prefer z and have the same low priority at z and y, so I put z ahead of y. In short: put x first (top true choice and reasonable priority), then w, then z, then y.
reasoning.Student D:
My true preference is x > y > w > z. I consider two strategic points:

1) Mechanism: If the system uses student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA), truthful reporting is a dominant strategy, so I should rank schools in my true order.

2) Competition & priorities: Most applicants favor y first, so y will be highly competitive. My priorities are relatively low at x and w (4) and a bit better at y and z (3). Even though I have slightly better priority at y, the heavy demand for y makes it unlikely I would win a seat there. Listing x first gives me the best chance of being matched to my top-choice (and is consistent with truthful play). Misreporting to try to game a different mechanism (e.g., ranking a less-preferred but less-contested school first) doesn’t improve my outcome given my low priorities at x/w and high demand for y.

Therefore I submit my true ranking: x > y > w > z.
